prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the development of long-acting GLP-1-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: I keep a single-part B014 with Drucker, Holst and Knudsen. The round-1 exchange did not change the scientific case: Holst's human incretin physiology, Drucker's proglucagon biology and extra-pancreatic actions, and Knudsen's albumin-binding acylation that turned a peptide with a half-life of minutes into a once-daily and then once-weekly medicine are three distinct, decisive and non-overlapping contributions. The mechanism has been stable for decades and the clinical claim rests on large independent randomized trials in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. The discovery is also mature enough that no one argues for waiting. My answer to the chair's first question is that the citation should name both the hormone's physiology and the therapeutic principle, because neither alone explains why this is a prize-worthy change in medicine. On the pairing question, the three-person cap decides it. Any second part would have to be funded from B014's names, and the only way to pair B014 with B016 or B006 is to cut a secure discoverer. The B014 core is stronger without that cut than a two-part prize would be with it.
statement.case_against: The residual weakness is still attribution at the edge of the story. Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active truncated peptide is a real contribution that I am leaving out, and Habener sits outside the supplied credit list but inside the same priority discussion. I am also choosing between two defensible principles, a discovery-first citation and a discovery-plus-design citation, and a reader could say that placing an industrial drug-design contribution beside two academic physiologists favours development over discovery. I cannot resolve the priority record from the supplied materials, and my judgment that Knudsen's contribution is more separable and more decisive than Mojsov's rests on that incomplete record. The incretin class also still has accumulating long-term safety data that I cannot verify here.

responses.point: She proposes Drucker, Holst and Mojsov as the cleaner discovery trio, and argues that replacing Mojsov with Knudsen makes the prize a hybrid: two people for the hormone's physiology and one for the drug.
responses.response: I agree it is a hybrid and I think the hybrid is accurate, because the achievement on the ballot is the physiology and its therapeutic exploitation, and the physiology part is already fully covered by Holst and Drucker. Adding Mojsov would give three people to the hormone side and none to the step that created the medicine. Your point that priority disputes should not decide the question alone is fair, and I do not exclude Mojsov on priority grounds. I exclude her because her contribution overlaps more with what Holst's group and Drucker's group established about the active forms than Knudsen's overlaps with anyone. If the committee wished a strictly discovery-only citation, your trio would be defensible and I would not call it wrong, but I would not choose it. I note that you say you would not block the Knudsen version.

responses.point: As chair he moved to Drucker, Holst and Knudsen in round 1, argued that a contested edge is not a contested core, and says he could accept Mojsov in place of Knudsen if the reasoning is stated.
responses.response: I agree with the distinction between a contested edge and a contested core, and it answers the concern that Habener's absence should hold the candidate back. Holst and Drucker are secure under any reading, so the open choice is only the third name. I would state the reasoning in the record as follows: the third place goes to the contribution that made the hormone a drug, because the citation names a discovery that became a medicine, and no discoverer's claim is judged smaller by that choice. I would resist treating the acceptability of the alternative as grounds to settle it by default. The committee should record that it considered Mojsov and chose on the scope of the citation, not on seniority or on how many members started in one place.

responses.point: He says translation has been recognised before when a discovery gave a new therapeutic principle, that Mojsov's claim is less separable from the physiology than the chair suggests, and that the SMN2 case rests on one drug and unproven durability against gene therapy.
responses.response: On GLP-1 I agree, and the precedent argument is the strongest one for Knudsen's place: acylation for albumin binding was a design principle that created a class, not routine optimisation. On B016 I accept part of your objection. The Krainer and Bennett credit is clean, but I conceded in round 1 and concede here that it is largely a single therapeutic story and that durability relative to gene therapy is not established. I still list it as an alternative because the splice-switching principle is general and proven in a fatal paediatric disease. I do not think it competes with B014 this year, and I agree with you that it could be a later prize.

responses.point: He asks whether pairing B014 with a second achievement is better than a single-topic prize and says the name limit would force awkward cuts, and he wants the citation wording, not seniority, to decide the Mojsov and Knudsen choice.
responses.response: I answered the pairing question above, and my view is that you identified the right constraint. With four credited names on B014 and a cap of three people in total, a two-part prize means at most two people on B014 or on the second part. For B006 that would mean naming perhaps one or two of June, Sadelain and Rosenberg, with Eshhar already outside the list, and I do not think that holds up. I also agree the wording should carry the decision, which is why my citation names both the physiology and the long-acting therapies explicitly. I share your discomfort about deciding by familiarity or by the unanimity of the opening ballots.

responses.point: He holds that a single B014 prize with Drucker, Holst and Knudsen is right, and notes that CAR-T is the strongest alternative but he would not pair it with GLP-1 unless the committee accepts the credit gap.
responses.response: I agree on both points, and on the Eshhar gap I would go further than the committee has so far. B006 is not only hard to pair with B014, it is the candidate I would most want to see fully resolved before a future round: either the citation is worded around costimulated, clinically validated CARs, with June and Sadelain as the clearest CAR-specific names, or Eshhar's original chimeric receptor concept has to be reflected in the credit. As it stands, Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer is a broader achievement than the CAR modality. For this vote I treat B006 as the strongest alternative and not as a rival to B014, and I thank you for stating that position plainly.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers a discovery-only citation naming Mojsov or a discovery-plus-design citation naming Knudsen as the third place, and whether the record states that reasoning explicitly.
Whether Habener's role in the proglucagon-derived peptide work should affect how the citation is worded even though he is outside the supplied credit list.
Whether B006 can be given a defensible credit without Eshhar and without conflating Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer with CAR design.
Long-term safety and outcome data for the newest GLP-1-based agents are still accumulating, and I cannot verify them from the supplied materials.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. My profile records the 2016 Science spatial transcriptomics paper and eight co-authored works with Rickard Sandberg, a fellow committee member, and I have no documented tie to any credited name on B014, B006 or B016. No recusal is requested, and I do not infer connections from shared Karolinska Institutet affiliation or from topic overlap.
